# Scaphoid fracture

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Scaphoid fracture*

[Original Article Link](/library/l30vif)

---

## Summary

The <u>scaphoid bone</u> is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. <u>Fractures</u> are most often localized in the middle third of the <u>scaphoid bone</u>. Generally, <u>scaphoid bone</u> <u>fractures</u> result when an individual falls onto the outstretched hand with a hyperextended and radially deviated wrist. <u>Pain</u> when applying pressure to the <u>anatomical snuffbox</u> is highly suggestive of a <u>scaphoid bone</u> <u>fracture</u>. <u>X-ray</u> is the initial test of choice for diagnosis. CT and <u>MRI</u> may be indicated if <u>x-ray</u> findings are negative but clinical suspicion is high. All suspected <u>scaphoid</u> <u>fractures</u> should be immobilized in a <u>thumb spica cast</u>. Definitive treatment can be nonoperative (i.e., wrist <u>immobilization</u>) or surgical (e.g., for <u>proximal</u> pole <u>fractures</u>). Complications include <u>nonunion</u> and <u>avascular necrosis</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Most common carpal bone <u>fracture</u> (50–80%) [[1]](/library/iWXJOC)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 15–19 years [[2]](/library/RWXlOC)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Clinical features

* History of falling onto the outstretched hand;  with a hyperextended and radially deviated wrist  [[4]](/library/_WX5LC)

* <u>Pain</u> when applying pressure to the <u>anatomical snuffbox</u> and scaphoid tubercle (a palpable bony prominence on the inferior <u>lateral</u> edge of the <u>scaphoid bone</u>)

* Minimal reduction in the <u>range of motion</u> (except in <u>dislocated fractures</u>)

* Decreased grip strength

* Painful pinching and grasping

* <u>Pain</u> can be induced through axial compression along the first <u>metacarpal</u> (scaphoid compression test).  [[4]](/library/_WX5LC)

## Diagnosis

<u>X-ray</u> is the best initial test; advanced imaging is only indicated in selected cases. [[5]](/library/redfZ60)




### <u>X-ray</u> [[5]](/library/redfZ60)[[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Indication: suspected <u>scaphoid</u> <u>fracture</u>

* Views: posteroanterior, <u>lateral</u>, oblique, and <u>scaphoid views</u>

* Findings

* Radiographic signs of <u>fractures</u>

* Displacement, bowing, or obliteration of the <u>scaphoid</u> fat pad





> [!TIP]
> Consider advanced imaging if initial <u>x-rays</u> are negative for <u>fractures</u>, as 15–20% of <u>scaphoid</u> <u>fractures</u> are undetectable on the initial <u>x-ray</u>. [[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)

### Advanced imaging [[5]](/library/redfZ60)[[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)




* Indications

* Suspected <u>occult fracture</u>  [[8]](/library/dfdoO60)

* Suspected associated <u>tendon</u> or <u>ligament injury</u>

* Preoperative planning for complicated injuries

* Modalities [[9]](/library/VfdGO60)

* Standard modalities: <u>MRI</u>, CT

* Additional modalities include <u>bone scintigraphy</u>  and <u>ultrasound</u>.  [[5]](/library/redfZ60)[[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* All suspected <u>scaphoid</u> <u>fractures</u>

* Provide <u>analgesia for acute fractures</u>.

* Immobilize in a <u>thumb spica cast</u> or <u>splint</u>.

* Arrange orthopedic follow-up within one week.

* Confirmed <u>fractures</u>: nonoperative or surgical management (depending on stability)

* Suspected <u>occult fractures</u>: <u>immobilization</u> with <u>x-ray</u> reevaluation after 10–14 days or advanced imaging [[5]](/library/redfZ60)





> [!WARNING]
> When <u>pain</u> occurs in the <u>anatomical snuffbox</u> after trauma, the injury should be treated as a suspected <u>scaphoid</u> <u>fracture</u> until proven otherwise.




### Nonoperative management [[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)




* Indications: Consider for all <u>stable fractures</u>. 

* Nondisplaced or minimally displaced <u>fractures</u> (< 1 mm)

* <u>Distal</u> pole <u>fractures</u>

* <u>Fractures</u> with normal intercarpal alignment

* Technique: <u>immobilization</u> in a short- or long-arm <u>thumb spica cast</u> for at least 6–8 weeks  [[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)





### Surgical management [[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)




* Indications

* General indications for <u>surgical fracture management</u>, e.g., <u>open fractures</u>, neurovascular compromise

* Displaced <u>fractures</u> (> 1 mm)

* <u>Proximal</u> pole <u>fractures</u>  [[6]](/library/WVdPtK0)

* <u>Carpal instability</u>

* Radiographic signs of instability, e.g., bone loss

* Older <u>fractures</u> (> 4 weeks)

* Technique: percutaneous or <u>open reduction and internal fixation</u>

---

## Complications

* <u>Avascular necrosis</u> (especially in <u>proximal</u> <u>fractures</u> that disrupt blood flow from branches of the <u>radial artery</u>) of the <u>scaphoid bone</u> in up to 50% of cases [[10]](/library/YdXnoC)

* <u>Nonunion</u> (especially in <u>proximal</u> <u>fractures</u>) in approx. 10%  [[11]](/library/adXQoC)

* Delayed union of <u>fracture</u> (more common in smokers)

* Instability among carpal <u>joints</u>

* Post-traumatic <u>arthritis</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Fractures</u> in the <u>distal</u> third tend to heal better because of the retrograde blood supply reaching the bone from the <u>distal</u> pole.
